newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia suspends party officials over corruption. [CORRECTED 15:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Croatia suspends party officials over corruption. [CORRECTED 15:38 GMT]

text.p: The Croatian government, its popularity dented by corruption allegations ahead of communal elections next year, has suspended 33 ruling party officials as a result of a fraud inquiry, state media reported on Friday.
President Franjo Tudjman has recently become concerned about the image of his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party's hierarchy after years of denying or ignoring suspected graft.

The HDZ majority in parliament was slashed to the minimum in a general election on October 29, 1995, at which voters registered their feelings about alleged HDZ abuses of Croatia's privatisation process and the publicly perceived arrogance and aloofness of party leaders.

Polls show the HDZ faces big losses -- with 25 percent or less of the vote -- in nationwide communal elections due next spring. A presidential poll is also due next year -- possibly in August, though no date has been set -- and opposition parties hope to pit a joint candidate against Tudjman.

An HDZ communique said the party presidency had debated the need to stamp out fraud and name those responsible for "malpractices and breaking of the law, especially in the process of privatisation and restructuring".
It said 33 officials had been suspended from party functions, but not government jobs if they had any, pending completion of a "disciplinary process", or investigation.

Among those affected were the former assistant defence minister, Josip Juras, and Martin Katicic, president of Privredna Banka, the largest state bank which has suffered huge losses as a result of uncollected loans to industries run by government officials.

Others included a former mayor of Zagreb, Branko Miksa, and his successor Marina Matulovic-Dropulic, who was appointed after Tudjman refused to recognise an opposition victory in Zagreb municipal elections that coincided with last year's general election. She has remained construction minister as well.
Matulovic-Dropulic released a statement through the official news agency Hina denying any wrongdoing.
She said she was not involved in any scheme to buy large volumes of privatisation shares at illegal discounts -- a key accusation levelled at some senior HDZ officials.
The other prominent HDZ official suspended was Kruno Peronja, prefect of Split county on the Adriatic seacoast.

Political analysts say the anti-corruption drive has both a domestic and a foreign context. The central government (corrects from "federal government") is keen to show it is building a legitimate free market economy so the country can qualify for links with 15-nation European Union.
The Council of Europe, antechamber of the EU, admitted Croatia as its 40th member state this week, five years after the HDZ-led republic declared independence from Yugoslavia.
The few Croatian newspapers not under HDZ control have been publishing accounts of privatisation fraud since Tudjman's nationalist movement ousted communists from power in 1990.

Hardly a week goes by without an expose by independent journalists of lucrative state properties being bought for pittances, widespread nepotism and other irregularities by Croats exploiting state contacts.

A conspicuous new-money elite has emerged while much of the pre-independence middle class has been reduced to near-poverty by hyperinflation and profiteering during the 1991-95 ethnic wars in the region of former Yugoslavia.

In another measure to ingratiate itself with ordinary Croats, the government on Friday announced it was indefinitely postponing a 22 percent value added tax which was to have been introduced at the start of next year.
